# Conclusions

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Plain-Language Summary
We built a two-stage hierarchical ICD-10 coder, reported strong results — and
then found that our synthetic benchmark was leaking the diagnostic answer into
the note text. Correcting the leak cut the headline accuracy by ~30% relative
and, more importantly, **reversed which model backbone is best**. The lasting
contribution of this work is therefore a cautionary one about evaluating
clinical-NLP systems on synthetic data.
:::

---

## Summary of Findings {#sec-conclusions-summary}

This study divides into a development phase on a benchmark we later found to be
compromised, and a corrected re-evaluation on de-leaked data. The findings
below are stated in their corrected form; numbers are de-leaked unless noted.

### Finding 1: The leakage that inflated and distorted the results

The certified redaction that produced our gold data removed ICD-10 *codes* from
the note text but left their human-readable *descriptions* in place. A note
labelled `M25.562` still contained "pain in left knee" — letting the model read
the answer rather than infer it. Removing this leakage dropped ClinicalBERT's
hierarchical end-to-end accuracy from a reported **85.8% to 59.2%** (~30%
relative), concentrated almost entirely in within-chapter code resolution. This
is the single most consequential fact in the study and the lens through which
every other result must be read.

### Finding 2: Leakage inverted the backbone ranking — the central result

On the leaky benchmark, Bio_ClinicalBERT appeared to beat Clinical ModernBERT
decisively (85.8% vs 48.8%), and we had concluded that "domain pretraining
outweighs architectural modernity." **On de-leaked data the ranking reverses:**
Clinical ModernBERT reaches **76.9%**, beating ClinicalBERT's 59.2% by ~18
points, and does so uniformly — winning 17 of 19 chapters. The leaked signal
was strong enough that the older model exploited it best, manufacturing an
apparent backbone conclusion that is the *opposite* of the truth on clean data.
A leaky benchmark did not merely inflate scores; it ranked the backbones
backwards.

### Finding 3: The hierarchical architecture requires warm initialisation

This lesson survives de-leaking because it concerns the training recipe rather
than the leaked signal. A cold-started Stage-2 collapses (≈11% E2E) despite a
near-perfect chapter router; warm-starting the resolvers from a flat ICD-10
classifier is necessary for the architecture to function. Both the leaky and
de-leaked regimes agree on this.

### Finding 4: Calibrated confidence enables selective automation — at a more modest operating point

Temperature scaling produces well-calibrated confidence scores (de-leaked ECE
0.039 for the best model), making a confidence threshold meaningful. On
de-leaked data the best model (Clinical ModernBERT) auto-codes 73.7% of cases
at 90.0% precision at τ = 0.7 — a more modest profile than the leaky figures
(86.4% / 95.6%) implied, but a defensible one resting on data that does not
leak the answer.

---

## The Z-Chapter: a Cautionary Sub-Story {#sec-conclusions-z}

The administrative Z-chapter was the hardest chapter, and on the leaky
benchmark Supervised Contrastive (SupCon) fine-tuning appeared to "solve" it —
lifting Z accuracy by +21.2pp and the system to 86.7%. **This result did not
survive de-leaking.** On clean data, SupCon yields a modest genuine improvement
on the Z resolver's validation accuracy (~6pp) that nearly vanishes at the
system level (+0.5pp, 59.2%→59.7%), and is small enough to be sensitive to the
data partition. The dramatic leaky gain was leakage, not contrastive learning.
This is a second, independent illustration of the same lesson: a leaky
benchmark can manufacture an algorithmic "win" that does not exist.

The technique is not without merit — a small real effect remains, and
contrastive objectives may still help where classes are genuinely
feature-similar — but the claim that SupCon solves the Z chapter is withdrawn.

---

## Real-World Validation {#sec-conclusions-real}

On 4,877 real MIMIC-IV discharge summaries, the de-leaked system scores **8.1%**
end-to-end (the leaky model scored 12.0%). Both collapse to near-floor, so the
synthetic-to-real gap is driven by **domain shift** and is largely independent
of leakage. Real notes use abbreviations, shorthand, copy-paste artefacts, and
institution-specific terminology absent from the synthetic training data.
Whatever the synthetic headline, neither model is usable on real notes without
domain adaptation.

---

## Reproducibility {#sec-conclusions-repro}

All de-leaked results use a content-addressed split (keyed by record id), so the
test partition is reproducible and identical across every model — which is what
makes the backbone comparison exact. The full chain (flat pre-training →
hierarchical training → calibration → evaluation, for each backbone, plus the
SupCon and MIMIC steps) is driven by a single tested orchestrator.

```bash
# Complete reproduction from scratch
uv run python scripts/run_full_deleaked_rebuild.py
# Total runtime: ~20 hours on Apple-silicon (MPS)
```

The orchestration logic, split logic, and pre-flight verification are covered
by 170 unit tests (no GPU required), added during the corrective work to ensure
the rebuild was trustworthy.

---

## Broader Context {#sec-conclusions-context}

Automated ICD-10 coding at the scale of the full billable code set remains
unsolved on real data. This study's contribution is less a coding system than a
methodological warning: **synthetic benchmarks for clinical NLP can leak the
answer in subtle, description-level ways that survive code-level redaction, and
the resulting distortion is not limited to inflated scores — it can invert
architectural conclusions and fabricate apparent algorithmic gains.** Reviewers
and practitioners should treat strong results on synthetic clinical data with
corresponding caution, and should test for description-level leakage explicitly,
not only for verbatim code leakage.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🎯 The Bottom Line

We set out to build an ICD-10 coder and report that it worked well. The more
useful result is what we found when we checked our own benchmark: a
description-level leak that inflated the headline from a true 59.2% to a
reported 85.8%, reversed the backbone ranking (Clinical ModernBERT, not
ClinicalBERT, is best on clean data), and manufactured a SupCon "win" that does
not exist. The architecture is sound and warm-starting is essential — but the
headline lesson is about evaluation, not architecture. Leaky synthetic
benchmarks can be confidently, measurably wrong.
:::
